chapter: The levee club and the St. Louis scene
title: Grabbed on the way to the levee
summary: On his way to the rough levee district with his horn bag, a stranger lifted Thomas off his feet.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: See what I mean. I should have explained that to you. Still living in Webster Groves with my family. You'd like to hear a little incident that happened?
In those days, you made a bag like these fellows nowadays, these manufacturers have trumpet bags. My mother that used to make my bag for me out of things/were left over.
Cloth of a kind. And I'd tell her I'd just as well

leave this so I could zip. Not the zip, you know, just put it open. I got my horn with me And the levee, and I feel good. We were rugged. It was very rugged country. That was a fur district. You know (fur district one is shoes) From ( ) Washington. ... walking down to the levee. So/night I'm feeling very good. I'm a boy around, I must be around 175 pounds, something like that. I'm in good shape. Everybody was happy at home, like that. And out of nowhere, a guy, somebody grabs me and lifts me off of my feet. Traction I need! You dig it I said, "Man, put me down.! He grabbed my horn Ain't putting no knife on me, you know, no gun. I said, "Put me down. What are you doing?" So he says, "Hey, little fellow, where are you going?" Little fellow? What the hell you think this is at that time(...) I said, "I'm going to work." And he says, "where you going"... I got a couple of dollars, you know. He said, "Now, I'm hungry." Now that weren't no robbery that was happening. You could walk with the rest of the cats. You might be in the way you know, rob some furs and some shoes, that kind, you know. Weren't no stick-up. The people there, you remember a fellow by the name of E. Simms Campbell? The cartoonist.
